scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Dance in Iran dates back to at least the 6th millennium BC, evidenced by artifacts from archaeological sites such as Tepe Sabz, Susa, and Tepe Sialk.
Early historic dances include Mithra worship involving bull sacrifice to promote vigor, described by Herodotus in the 5th century BC.
Over time, foreign occupations (Greeks, Arabs, Mongols) and political instability caused the decline of some dance traditions.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Iranian dances serve multiple social and spiritual functions: communal celebration in weddings and festivals; ritual healing and exorcism in trance dances like Baluchi le’b guati; warrior training in combat dances; and artistic expression in court and social improvisational dances.
Dance can symbolize cultural identity, spiritual connection, and social cohesion.
Restrictions on public dance after 1979 shifted many practices to private or diaspora contexts.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Iranian dance includes four main categories: chain or line dances performed in circles or lines often holding hands or waists; solo improvisational dances featuring delicate hand and arm movements with expressive facial gestures; war or combat dances mimicking fighting or training warriors, such as the zurkhaneh footwork dance Raghs-e-Pa; and ritual or spiritual dances like Sufi sama involving chanting and trance.
Watch for Wrist Circles, Hand Waves, Finger Snapping (Peshkan).

Formation: Circle or line formations for chain dances; solo space for improvisation; paired or small group formations in combat dances

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The most common rhythm for Iranian dance music is 6/8 meter, known as shir-e mâdar, with melodic and rhythmic variations including 7/8 in some styles like Motrebi.
Traditional instruments include Persian percussion and melodic instruments supporting both communal and solo dances.
Listen for the Persian percussion instruments, Traditional melodic instruments.
The pulse is 6/8 commonly, with variations including 7/8.
Music features cyclical 6/8 rhythms with melodic ornamentation, supporting both communal and solo dance forms; vocal chanting or singing may accompany ritual or court dances.

Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Cyclical rhythmic patterns emphasizing melody and dance steps; shir-e mâdar rhythm

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes vary widely by dance style and region.
Tribal dances like Basseri feature colorful traditional clothes, while classical Persian court dances use rich silks, brocades, and flowing long skirts.
Social dances may involve simpler attire suitable for parties or weddings.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Notable dancers include Jamileh, a Los Angeles-based belly dancer; Farzaneh Kaboli, an Iranian actress and dancer; Mohammad Khordadian, an Iranian-American dancer; Shahrokh Moshkin-Ghalam, a Paris-based modern dancer; and Azita Sahebjam, director of the Vancouver Pars National Ballet.
Ballet Afsaneh is a prominent female dance troupe focused on Persian culture in the San Francisco Bay Area.

Iran’s ethnic diversity produces many regional dance styles: Bandari dance from the southern Persian Gulf with Arabic influences; Bojnordi dance from northeast Iran with finger snapping; Choob bazi stick dances from southwestern Iran; Yalli, an Azerbaijani folk dance; and Baluchi spiritual dances like le’b guati.
Iranian dance traditions descend from ancient ritual and court dances documented since prehistory and classical antiquity.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Iranian dance is parent of Middle Eastern dance: Iranian dance is a regional subset of Middle Eastern dance traditions.
Iranian dance is sibling of Azerbaijani dances: Shared cultural and ethnic influences, especially in northern Iran.
Iranian dance is shares music of Persian theatre: Traditional Persian theatre incorporates dance and music elements.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Certain ritual dances, such as Sufi sama and Baluchi trance healing dances, are sacred and involve trance states; these are restricted to initiated practitioners and should not be imitated by outsiders.

wardrobe.from_sources: Costumes vary widely by dance style and region. Tribal dances like Basseri feature colorful traditional clothes, while classical Persian court dances use rich silks, brocades, and flowing long skirts. Social dances may involve simpler attire suitable for parties or weddings. Performances occur in diverse settings including private homes, weddings, cultural festivals, traditional gymnasiums (zurkhaneh), and diaspora cultural centers. Some ritual dances are restricted and performed only by initiated practitioners.
